Cyrillic-script variants and Montenegrin-specific orthography (izvještaj vs izveštaj, rješenje vs rešenje) were not systematically exercised, and no Albanian-language search was run despite a significant Albanian-speaking minority.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Re-run key queries with ekavian and Cyrillic variants and a small Albanian glossary (prokurimi publik, tenderi, ankesa) to test for missed local sources.

coverage_gaps.description: EU-level and regional aggregators that mirror Montenegrin notices — TED, Balkan Tender Watch's regional database, and Open Contracting Data Standard mirrors — were not investigated for ME coverage.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Test whether Montenegro publishes OCDS data or appears in TED for EU-funded procurements, which would give a structured alternative to scraping CEJN.

coverage_gaps.description: Sector buyers not yet mapped to a procurement URL: CGES (transmission), Željeznička infrastruktura CG and Željeznički prevoz CG (rail), Montecargo, Barska plovidba, Regionalni vodovod Crnogorsko primorje, Zavod za zapošljavanje, plus the ~20 municipal ViK and Čistoća utilities outside Podgorica and Bar.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Parse the newest UJN 'Lista naručilaca' PDF into a buyer table, mark the sektorski naručioci, then resolve each to a domain and test the observed URL patterns (/javne-nabavke/, /category/tenderi-i-javne-nabavke/, /javni-pozivi/, /servis-gradana/otvoreni-grad/javne-nabavke/, and dedicated javnenabavke.* subdomains).

coverage_gaps.description: The authoritative central portal (CeJN) is a JavaScript SPA and was not readable by plain fetch. Whether it exposes contracting-authority filtering, CPV codes, award values, bulk export or an RSS/JSON API is unknown.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Run one headless-browser session against cejn.gov.me/tenders with the network tab captured, identify the backing JSON endpoints, and document filter parameters — especially the naručilac identifier — before designing any collection.

coverage_gaps.description: Coverage of sr-Cyrl (Cyrillic) renderings is untested. FZOCG serves pages in both Latin and Cyrillic script, and other public funds may too; a Latin-only crawler could silently miss or duplicate content.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Add script-transliteration normalisation (sr-Latn <-> sr-Cyrl) to both query generation and deduplication for the funds and any site with a script switcher.

coverage_gaps.description: Award notices and contract values are under-covered relative to calls for tender. Only fragmentary award data was found (CEDIS meter tender values and bidder counts came from trade press, not a primary award feed; the Monteput toll award likewise).
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Establish a separate award-notice ('obavještenje o ishodu postupka', 'ugovor o javnoj nabavci') collection track and, where SOE pages are stale, use the Zakon o slobodnom pristupu informacijama (FOI) route to the named procurement officer from the UJN 'Lista službenika'.

coverage_gaps.description: Historical depth is unclear for every SOE page examined. Pošta's page showed only 2020 items; Luka Bar's category paginates but the depth of the archive was not probed; no site was confirmed to retain multi-year notice history.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Probe pagination depth per site and, for stale or shallow sites, back-fill from the Wayback Machine before establishing the live monitoring cadence.

coverage_gaps.description: Indirect/revealing sources are thin for this cell — SOE annual reports, board (upravni odbor) minutes, state-audit reports (Državna revizorska institucija) on SOEs, and the funds' 'analitičke kartice' spend ledgers were noted but not systematically sourced.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Add a pass specifically for DRI (state audit) reports on SOEs and for the funds' analytical-card/spend disclosures, which reveal incumbent suppliers and actual spend where tender pages are silent.

coverage_gaps.description: CEJN (cejn.gov.me) could not be read without JavaScript, so CBCG's national-portal procurement record — plans, tender documentation, award-outcome notices — remains unmapped.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Run a headless-browser session against cejn.gov.me/tenders, filter naručilac = 'Centralna banka Crne Gore', and capture the XHR/JSON endpoints the SPA calls so collection can poll JSON directly. Also test whether an anonymous account unlocks fuller search.

coverage_gaps.description: CBCG's annual procurement plan (plan javnih nabavki) and any contract register were not located in any public location.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: File a Zakon o slobodnom pristupu informacijama request to CBCG for the current and prior-year procurement plans and the register of concluded contracts; in parallel search CEJN, which typically hosts contracting-authority plans, and check DRI audit reports which routinely quote plan figures.

coverage_gaps.description: How the RTS/X payment system and the TIPS Clone platform were actually contracted is unresolved. The TIPS Clone is World Bank financed (EUR 8m) and technically supplied via Banca d'Italia under Eurosystem auspices, which may mean much of it never passes through a competitive tender at all.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Retrieve the World Bank project P509405 Procurement Plan and STEP contract awards, and check whether CBCG-Banca d'Italia cooperation is governed by a bilateral agreement published in Službeni list Crne Gore rather than a tender. Determine which components remain open to third-party vendors (connectivity, UX/marketing, security, integration).

coverage_gaps.description: Službeni list Crne Gore (Official Gazette) was not queried in this pass. CBCG decisions, operating rules for the payment system, and international cooperation agreements are promulgated there.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Add sluzbenilist.me to the source set and search for CBCG payment-system decisions and any agreement with Banca d'Italia, the ECB or the World Bank; these define the legal frame within which CBCG procures.

coverage_gaps.description: Vendor-side sources were not scouted: banknote/coin processing and authentication suppliers (e.g. Giesecke+Devrient, Koenig & Bauer Banknote Solutions, Toshiba, Glory, CPS/cash-cycle integrators) and payments-platform integrators publish customer references, press releases and case studies that reveal CBCG contracts after award.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Build a vendor watchlist for cash-processing and payment-infrastructure suppliers active in the Western Balkans and monitor their news/reference pages for Montenegro mentions; the cma.se hit for 'Central Bank of Montenegro' seen in search results is an example of this vendor-case-study class and should be evaluated.

coverage_gaps.description: Searching was done in Montenegrin/Serbian Latin script only. Cyrillic-script variants ('Централна банка Црне Горе', 'јавне набавке') and Italian-language sources (Banca d'Italia's own TIPS Clone communications and procurement) were not queried.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Re-run key queries in Cyrillic transliteration and add Italian-language queries against bancaditalia.it for TIPS Clone partner-country arrangements and supplier selection.

coverage_gaps.description: Historical depth is thin. The CBCG tender page shows a sparse and uneven archive (2026, 2025, 2023, 2019, 2018) with apparent gaps, and no archived snapshots were checked.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Backfill from the Internet Archive (web.archive.org) for cbcg.me/me/javnost-rada/tenderi-i-oglasi across 2015-2026 to recover notices since removed, and cross-check against nabavke.com's CEJN document mirror.

coverage_gaps.description: Council of Europe Development Bank (CEB), IFC, and bilateral donors beyond KfW (e.g. Austrian ADA, Italian Cooperation, USAID successors, Swiss SECO) were not systematically checked for Montenegro financial-sector tenders.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Run a dedicated pass over CEB, SECO, ADA and Italian Cooperation procurement pages filtered for Montenegro and financial/PFM sectors.

coverage_gaps.description: The procurement plan for the World Bank SEPA/TIPS-clone project (indicative contract packages, methods, timing) was not extracted; only the PAD was located.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Fetch the PAD PDF procurement annex and the project's STEP-fed procurement-plan page to enumerate forthcoming payment-system contract packages and the implementing agency (Central Bank of Montenegro / Ministry of Finance).

coverage_gaps.description: ECEPP and UNGM lack confirmed, ToU-compliant bulk/API access paths; only per-notice URLs were observed.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Check ECEPP and UNGM terms of use and any official API/RSS or notification-subscription feature; prefer official email alerts over scraping where no API exists.

coverage_gaps.description: The Montenegrin-language vocabulary for donor tenders was only partially harvested (EU tenderi, poziv za dostavljanje ponuda, obavještenje o ugovoru, ugovaranje, IPA, digitalizacija plaćanja); no controlled glossary with transliterations and noisy-term flags was produced.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Build a sr/me glossary from ujn.gov.me 'EU tenderi' items and CFCU documents; flag 'nabavka' and 'tender' as high-noise generic terms requiring donor-name qualifiers.

coverage_gaps.description: Historical award archives (who won past donor-funded Montenegro financial/IT contracts) were only touched via Finances One; TED and ECEPP award histories were not mined.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Backfill 2015-2026 contract award notices from TED bulk data (place of performance ME) and ECEPP award notices to build a supplier/competitor map.

coverage_gaps.description: Official domains for Universal Capital Bank, Adriatic Bank, Lovćen banka, Addiko Podgorica and Razvojna banka/IRF were inferred from branding rather than confirmed from an authoritative register during this run.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Fetch the CBCG 'Banke u Crnoj Gori' / register-of-banks pages first and use them as the single source of truth for every bank domain before any crawl is scheduled.

coverage_gaps.description: CKB banka, the market leader and the most important private buyer in the cell, was never successfully read because of a TLS chain failure.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Re-attempt with a headless browser or a client configured with a full CA bundle / AIA chasing; if it still fails, capture the certificate chain and record the site as bot-defended-but-live rather than dead.

coverage_gaps.description: Searching was carried out in Serbian/Montenegrin and English as required, but no searching was done in Turkish (for Ziraat's parent-group announcements), Slovenian (for NLB Group sourcing), German (Erste Group) or Hungarian (OTP Group, CKB's owner). Group-level procurement for four of the largest ME banks is likely documented only in the parent's language.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Add a parent-group language pass: OTP (hu), NLB (sl), Erste (de), Addiko (de), Ziraat (tr) — searching each group's supplier/procurement and press pages for Montenegro references.

coverage_gaps.description: No supplier-side registry or contract-registry route was explored for Montenegro: the Central Registry of Business Entities (CRPS), court/insolvency filings, and bank annual-report notes on outsourcing and related-party supplier transactions were not searched in this run.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Add a dedicated pass over CRPS company filings and over each bank's audited annual report (Izvještaji sections), where outsourcing arrangements and material supplier contracts are frequently disclosed under regulatory outsourcing rules.

coverage_gaps.description: Bank social and recruitment channels were not searched. LinkedIn job posts for procurement/vendor-management roles, and bank LinkedIn/Facebook posts announcing technology partners, are a common leak route in small markets. Hipotekarna banka's active Facebook presence was observed but not mined.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Add a LinkedIn/Facebook monitoring pass per bank, focused on procurement job ads (which reveal the sourcing function and its scope) and partner-announcement posts.

coverage_gaps.description: Of the candidates listed, only nlb.me, hipotekarnabanka.com and erstebank.me were actually fetched. All other URLs come from search-result metadata or reasoned inference and carry no liveness claim.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Run the deterministic liveness pass over every URL in this slice before any is promoted to a monitored source, and downgrade the confidence of any that 404 (moved) while retaining any that 403/timeout (bot-defended).

coverage_gaps.description: ZIRAAT Bank Montenegro AD Podgorica's own website could not be identified in this pass (only SWIFT directories, thebanks.eu, the Montenegrin securities-market entry at scmn.me and a directory listing at Bulevar Ivana Crnojevića 101, Podgorica). Without the domain, the hypothesised /ihaleler-style subsidiary tender page cannot be probed.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Resolve the official domain via the CBCG registar banaka entry and the scmn.me issuer record, then probe /ihaleler, /tenderi, /nabavke, /javni-pozivi and the Turkish-language variants.

coverage_gaps.description: The vendor side was not systematically scouted. Payments and banking-technology suppliers (processors, card personalisation bureaux, ATM/self-service, core banking) routinely publish 'selected by <Group> across N markets' press releases naming Montenegro, which is frequently the only public trace of a group framework agreement.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Add a vendor-newsroom sweep as a distinct source family: monitor the press pages and case-study libraries of the main CEE/SEE banking-technology suppliers, filtered on the five parent-group names plus Montenegro/Podgorica/CKB.

coverage_gaps.description: EU/EBRD/IFC and other IFI procurement-notice channels were not searched. Where a parent group runs a donor- or IFI-financed programme (digitalisation, green lending platforms) that touches the Montenegrin subsidiary, procurement is competed under IFI rules and published — a genuinely public tender feed in a cell that otherwise has none.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Scout EBRD and IFC procurement notice boards and EU TED for notices naming the parent groups or their SEE subsidiaries as implementing parties.

coverage_gaps.description: The two most operationally valuable channels (the OTP SAP Ariba buyer instance and any Erste equivalent) are invitation-gated. Automated collection is impossible and probably impermissible; there is no public projection of their event calendars.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Treat supplier registration as a business action, not a collection action: escalate the decision to register on each parent's e-sourcing platform, and record registration status per parent as a coverage attribute of this cell.

coverage_gaps.description: Erste Group Procurement's e-sourcing platform was not identified. Searches did not establish whether EGP runs SAP Ariba, Jaggaer, Coupa or an in-house tool, so the registration path for the largest centrally-managed spend pool in this cell is unknown.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Fetch the supplier-document subpages linked from the EGP page (general terms, NDA, audit questionnaire) — the platform name and supplier-portal URL are typically stated inside those PDFs — or contact EGP directly.

coverage_gaps.description: No German-language parent-procurement glossary was built for Erste and Addiko beyond incidental terms observed on the EGP page (Lieferantenmanagement, Beschaffung, Tochtergesellschaften). Ausschreibung, Vergabe, Rahmenvereinbarung, Lieferantenportal and Einkauf were not systematically searched.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Run a dedicated de-language pass over erstegroup.com and addiko.com using Ausschreibung / Vergabe / Rahmenvereinbarung / Lieferantenportal / Einkauf before concluding no Austrian parent tender channel exists.

coverage_gaps.description: The DORA Register-of-Information regime covers EU-supervised entities, so it captures Erste, NLB and Addiko group vendor inventories but not OTP's Montenegrin subsidiary, and Montenegro itself is outside the EU supervisory perimeter. The CBCG's own outsourcing/ICT-third-party notification requirements were not investigated.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Scout CBCG regulations and any register or notification obligation for bank outsourcing and ICT third-party arrangements in Montenegro — a possible local mirror of the DORA register covering exactly the group-sourced vendors.

coverage_gaps.description: Card personalisation and card switch/processing suppliers to Montenegrin banks were not identified from the supplier side in this pass.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Run dedicated sr/en queries ('personalizacija kartica', 'procesiranje kartičnih transakcija', 'kartični procesor Crna Gora') and check regional processors (ASEE/Payten, Halcom, Bankart, Multicard, First Data/Fiserv successors) for Montenegro references; inspect bank card T&Cs which often name the processor.

coverage_gaps.description: No per-bank vendor attribution table exists yet for the ~11-15 licensed Montenegrin banks.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Build a bank-by-bank grid (CKB/OTP, NLB Podgorica, Erste, Hipotekarna, Lovćen, Prva banka, Universal Capital Bank, Addiko, Adriatic Bank, Zapad banka, Ziraat) and populate it from app-store package IDs, web-tech fingerprints, privacy-policy processor lists and job ads before relying on press releases.

coverage_gaps.description: Local vendor primary websites (Logate, ČIKOM, Amplitudo, Printec Montenegro) were identified but their reference/news pages were not directly retrieved, so their customer lists are unread.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Fetch each vendor domain with a browser-grade collector; harvest 'Reference/Klijenti/Projekti/Vijesti' sections and snowball each named institution.

coverage_gaps.description: LinkedIn is repeatedly the richest supplier-announcement channel for this market but is platform-gated and was only sampled indirectly.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Establish a compliant LinkedIn monitoring routine (manual review or licensed tooling) for Printec, ASEE/Payten, Monri, Logate, ČIKOM and Montenegrin bank pages.

coverage_gaps.description: Vendor claims are unverified against buyer-side award records (complementary cells 7-8).
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Join vendor-announced wins to Montenegrin e-procurement award notices (CJN / ejn.gov.me) and to CRPS company-registry entity data, flagging vendor claims with no corresponding public award as private-bank contracts.

coverage_gaps.description: Cash-in-transit, cash-centre and ATM cash-management operators in Montenegro are entirely unmapped, as is the licensing register for private security agencies that would list them.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Query the Ministry of Interior (gov.me) for the register of licensed security agencies ('agencije za zaštitu lica i imovine'), and check bank annual reports and CEJN awards for named CIT contractors.

coverage_gaps.description: The card-processing layer for Montenegro was not resolved: it is unclear which processors (in-house bank platforms, regional processors, or group processors of foreign bank parents such as OTP/CKB, NLB, Erste, Addiko, Ziraat) issue and acquire for each institution.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Read each bank's annual report and card general terms for the named processor, and check the CBCG Register of Payment Systems plus Payten/Nexi/other regional processor reference lists.

coverage_gaps.description: The CEJN procurement portal's tender and award listings were identified but not queried with payments-specific keywords, so it is unknown whether it exposes structured search, CPV filtering, or an API.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Run a structured probe of cejn.gov.me/tenders with terms bankomat, POS terminal, platne kartice, platni promet, gotovina, procesiranje; document pagination, filters and any machine-readable endpoint before building a collector.

coverage_gaps.description: No Montenegro-specific tender aggregator or paid procurement-alert service was identified as an alternative to the state portal.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Test regional aggregators (e.g. TED for EU-funded ME notices, regional Balkan tender-alert vendors) and record licensing/ToS terms for redistribution.

coverage_gaps.description: Partnership and supplier-selection announcements for ME payment actors likely live on LinkedIn and Facebook company pages rather than websites (Montenegro Transfers was observed publishing WU pricing on Facebook), but no social-channel inventory was built.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Build a per-actor social-handle registry for licensed PIs, ATM operators and ICT Cortex fintech members, and assess ToS-compliant monitoring options.

coverage_gaps.description: The World Bank TIPS-clone/SEPA modernisation project was identified only via a press release; the project ID, procurement plan and any published contract awards were not retrieved.
coverage_gaps.recommended_action: Locate the project record on projects.worldbank.org and pull its procurement plan and STEP contract-award notices, which name winning suppliers for payments infrastructure.

briefs: Montenegro's A2 landscape has an unusually clean primary spine: since 1 January 2021 every stage of a public procurement - plan, javni poziv, tenderska dokumentacija, decisions, complaints and contracts - must run through CeJN (cejn.gov.me), the Belit-built, EU IPA-funded national e-procurement system operated by the Directorate for Public Procurement Policy (ujn.gov.me), with the pre-2021 record still searchable free of charge on the legacy eTender portal (portalujn.gov.me). The practical obstacle is not availability but machinability: CeJN is a JavaScript-rendered application with no discovered API, feed or bulk export, and its notice text is not indexed by general search engines, so payments lots cannot be found by web search - collection will need a headless browser or the commercial mirror nabavke.com, which rehosts CeJN tender documents under /tdoc-cejn/. Three material blind spots sit outside the portal: simple procurements below EUR 15,000 (many POS/terminal orders) that surface only in semi-annual authority reports; the Central Bank's own tenderi-i-oglasi page; and IFI-financed payments infrastructure - most notably the World Bank's July 2025 EUR 8m TIPS Clone / SEPA alignment project for CBCG, which will procure under Bank rules through Finances One and STEP rather than CeJN. Outcome and dispute detail is best recovered from the appeals commission's rjesenja at kontrola-nabavki.me and from State Audit Institution reports at dri.co.me.

Montenegro's outcome side is legally centralised in CEJN (cejn.gov.me), the state e-procurement system that must carry annual plans, award decisions, concluded contracts and execution reports — but it is a client-rendered SPA that yields nothing to a plain fetch, so the practical harvesting route is the private mirror nabavke.com, which serves the same CEJN documents at stable, indexable URLs (a confirmed pattern: /tdoc-cejn/documents/{id}-...-Odluka_o_izboru_najpovoljnije_ponude_{id}.pdf). Around that core sit three complementary channels: the appeals body kontrola-nabavki.me, whose rulings expose contested awards and losing bidders; UJN's annual Izvještaj o javnim nabavkama plus DRI audits and Institut alternativa/MANS commentary, which quantify and critique the contract population (~EUR 990m contracted in 2025, 12.44% of GDP); and TED for EU/IPA-financed Montenegrin award notices in structured form. Two structural constraints define the collector design: sector-relevant awards are effectively invisible to keyword web search and must be retrieved by CPV code and by contracting authority (CBCG above all), and private commercial banks fall entirely outside the procurement law, so for them no award register exists and vendor selections can only be inferred from bank saopštenja and trade press.

Montenegro's pointer layer for A2 is unusually well-formed on the financial-regulator side: CBCG publishes a compact set of official registers (banks; payment systems; payment institutions and agents; e-money institutions and agents; plus a revoked-authorisation negative list), and CRPS — reachable via pretraga.crps.me, crps.me and efirma.tax.gov.me — is the master company register, now carrying the beneficial-ownership register inside it since 2021. On the procurement side the enumerable populations exist but sit behind the CEJN/ESJN e-procurement system (registered ponuđači and the naručilac roster) with ujn.gov.me as the policy and reporting front end; AZZK holds the state-aid and de-minimis registers but appears to gate them behind an access request. The critical miss is fiscalisation: no public list of approved fiscal-device/POS software producers surfaced despite mandatory local-language searching, so the terminal supply chain currently has to be reconstructed indirectly from vendor self-declaration sites plus procurement awards — closing that gap by going directly to the tax authority should be the next action for this cell.

Montenegro's third-party tender-aggregation layer splits into three tiers: strong local/regional commercial services (eKapija Tenderi with its twice-daily bulletin, TenderiLIVE across ME/BA/RS, and the ME-specific eTenderi.me with competitor win-rate analytics and a State Commission appeals-decision archive), a horizontal global aggregator family (MontenegroTenders, TendersOnTime, TendersInfo, GlobalTenders) of lower and largely unverified quality, and an IFI/donor tier (EBRD ECEPP, WBIF, UNGM/UNDP, DevelopmentAid) that carries the donor-financed contracts the national CeJN portal never shows in the same form. Free structured alternatives are thin: opendata.gov.me exposes tender-tagged datasets and CeJN is the official baseline, but Montenegro is absent from opentender.eu/DIGIWHIST and no open-source CeJN scraper exists, so machine-readable ME procurement history effectively has to be bought or built. Pointer sources — Balkan Tender Watch (with MANS and Institute Alternative), the OCDS Data Registry, and the 2024 MAPS e-procurement assessment — are the best free routes to actor names, data-publication limits and known transparency failures such as unreported post-award contract amendments. No banking- or payments-specific vertical exists for this market, and every commercial platform's pricing, redistribution rights and incremental recall over the free baseline remain unverified.

Montenegro's audit-and-watchdog layer for procurement is small, well-defined and unusually productive: the State Audit Institution (DRI) anchors it with a two-decade archive of regularity, performance and — importantly for this run — dedicated information-system audits that name systems, vendors and IT-governance failures, while the Agency for Prevention of Corruption (ASK) adds annual/quarterly integrity and conflict-of-interest reporting. On the civil-society side, Institut alternativa supplies the quantitative work (shares of spending via direct agreements, urgent and shortened procedures, simple purchases, per-institution breakdowns) plus two NGO-built spending databases (mojnovac.me, mojgrad.me), MANS supplies FOI-extracted contracts that surface in the gov.me and parliamentary 'approved access' archives, and CGO, CIN-CG and the regional Balkan Tender Watch coalition fill in municipal, investigative and cross-country benchmarking angles; SIGMA/OECD and the OGP IRM provide external, methodologically consistent assessment. The key practical caveats: DRI's site failed TLS verification on every fetch attempt in this pass (almost certainly a certificate-chain issue on our side, not a dead source — do not mark it dead), MANS's procurement category index renders far thinner than the organisation's real output, and no watchdog product was found that targets banking or payment-sector IT procurement specifically. For the banking/payments scope this cell should therefore be worked entity-first — pulling DRI audits of financially-relevant auditees and grepping them for 'informacioni sistem' line items and supplier names — rather than topic-first.

Montenegro's media channel for tender and contract intelligence splits into three tiers: a small set of open, directly-confirmed local publishers that actually carry procurement detail (Bankar.me for banking-sector specificity, Investitor.me for central-bank equipment tenders, Dan for aggregate procurement-accountability numbers, and MANS as the NGO watchdog whose documents feed the press), a set of flagship dailies the cell brief names (Vijesti, Pobjeda, CdM, RTCG) that my searches never surfaced directly and which must be verified by live fetch before being trusted, and a layer of paywalled aggregators and regional/English outlets (eKapija, Tenderi Live, SeeNews, Bloomberg Adria, montenegrobusiness.eu) useful for corroboration but not for unlicensed automated collection. The clearest confirmed signal patterns are cancelled and legally challenged tenders — Montenegro was reported as the Western Balkans record-holder for annulled procedures, and a worked ANPR software case shows the discriminatory-documentation complaint template — plus institutional payment-infrastructure milestones (CBCG instant payments, EPC licence, treasury equipment tender) that precede procurement. Notably, no media report of a Montenegrin commercial bank procuring an information system was found in local-language search, which supports the cell's premise that private-bank contracts surface only obliquely and suggests future queries should target vendor-side and signing-ceremony language rather than tender vocabulary. The largest remaining gaps are regional ICT/fintech trade press, the banks' own press and tender pages, and Cyrillic-script querying, none of which this run reached before the search budget ran out.

Montenegro's weak-signal layer is small but unusually legible: with roughly a dozen licensed banks, a single dominant conference (INFINTECH, run by local software house Logate at Porto Montenegro) and one dominant ATM/POS servicer (Payten/ASEE, which publicly states its installed base), the vendor-to-bank map can largely be reconstructed without any procurement notice. The highest-yield channels found are conference sponsor/agenda pages, bank careers pages plus the national job boards (zaposli.me, posao.crna.gora.me, pazar3.me, prekoveze.me) with bankar.me acting as a durable archive of expired vacancy ads, and app-store package metadata that leaks each bank's digital-banking and SmartPOS supplier. Capex intent is retrievable from CBCG's bank financial-statement repository and from SCMN/Montenegroberza issuer prospectuses, both of which require PDF mining rather than a feed. The main uncovered ground is vendor partner-locator pages for hardware and core-banking brands, the non-bank PSP population, and LinkedIn, which is login-walled and ToS-restricted and therefore must be handled by manual analyst review rather than collection.

Montenegro's procurement legal framework is unusually well centralised for a small market: the Directorate for Public Procurement Policy at the Ministry of Finance (ujn.gov.me) publishes the consolidated Zakon o javnim nabavkama (Sl. list CG 074/19, 003/23, 011/23) together with its bylaws, contracting-authority lists and annual reports, while the CEJN platform (cejn.gov.me), built by Belit under an EC/IPA-funded project, is the mandated publication venue and therefore the single point of failure for every downstream notice cell. The reform pipeline is dated and specific rather than speculative: Chapter 5 closing benchmarks have been assessed as met, with binding commitments to amend the procurement and anti-corruption laws and to add a red-flag irregularity module to the e-procurement system by Q2 2026, alongside a separate Ministry of Finance track toward mandatory e-invoicing using a Serbian-licensed centralised platform phased over 2025-2026. Interpretation of the rules is carried by the Komisija za zaštitu prava u postupcima javnih nabavki decision archive and, independently, by SIGMA/OECD assessments and Institut alternativa watchdog research; commercial legal databases (paragraf.me, me.propisi.net) and law-firm guides are useful but demonstrably lag, with the CMS Montenegro chapter still describing a superseded review body and voluntary e-procurement. The main blind spots this run leaves open are the official gazette itself, the state audit institution, primary EU Chapter 5 documents, and the exemption regimes (bilateral intergovernmental agreements, defence/security, PPP) under which contracts legally never appear on CEJN at all.

Montenegro's procurement oversight layer is unusually well-suited to source tracking: the appeals body (Komisija za zaštitu prava u postupcima javnih nabavki) publishes a filterable, full-text-searchable decision database at kontrola-nabavki.me that names contracting authorities, complainants and winning bidders in contested lots, and its decisions are appealable to the Upravni sud whose judgments are also published. The policy side sits with the Direktorat za politiku javnih nabavki (ujn.gov.me plus gov.me/mif), which issues the annual national procurement reports carrying value-by-category aggregates — though the series is split across two hosts and incomplete, and the Commission's own work reports have no stable index. The statutory publication system CEJN (cejn.gov.me) is the join key linking appeals back to tender values, but its anonymous-access depth is unverified and its legacy predecessor is login-walled. Secondary calibration comes from DRI audits (including genuine IT-system audits), SIGMA/MAPS/EC assessments, and watchdogs MANS and Institut alternativa; no source offers a banking/payments-specific filter, so CPV and sr/en keyword filtering must be built collector-side.

Montenegro's SOE and utility buyers split their publication between the legally authoritative central portal (CeJN, cejn.gov.me) and their own websites, and the split is uneven enough that neither alone gives coverage: EPCG, CEDIS, Luka Bar, Aerodromi Crne Gore and Air Montenegro all maintain live self-published tender surfaces (Air Montenegro even runs a dedicated javnenabavke.* subdomain), while Pošta Crne Gore's own procurement page appears frozen around 2020 and Monteput and several municipal utilities publish no procurement index at all. The payments-relevant signal in this cell is concentrated in four buyers — Pošta (counter payment services, card terminals, in-branch ATMs, remittance partners), Monteput (cash, card and electronic toll collection), Aerodromi Crne Gore (public calls to place ATMs at Podgorica and Tivat) and EPCG/CEDIS (bill collection and mass metering) — each of which procures under the separate 'sektorski naručilac' utilities regime defined in the Zakon o javnim nabavkama. The critical enabling sources are the UJN 'Lista naručilaca' and 'Lista službenika' PDFs, which give an authoritative buyer roster plus a named procurement officer per buyer, and CeJN itself, which is live but JavaScript-rendered and returned only an app shell to a plain fetch — a tooling obstacle to solve, not a dead end. English-language search was near-useless here, collapsing into tender-resale SEO farms; every primary source in this slice was reached through Montenegrin-language queries anchored on the buyer's proper name.

CBCG's procurement footprint is genuinely split across three channels, and only one of them is obvious. Its own site carries a live but sparse 'Tenderi i oglasi' page — the richest cell-specific find, currently listing instant-payments (TIPS Clone) connectivity, pre-implementation technical support and UX/marketing calls alongside jubilee-coin and construction notices — while offering no procurement plan, no contract register and no dedicated 'javne nabavke' section at all. The national CEJN portal is the statutory home for its domestic procedures but is a JavaScript application that yielded nothing to a plain fetch, so it is currently uncollectable without headless rendering. Most consequentially, the flagship purchases bypass both: the CBCG treasury and cash-processing equipment tender (banknote and coin processing, euro anti-counterfeiting, gold testing; deadline 7 October 2026) runs on the EU Funding & Tenders Portal under EC-ENEST references administered by the Ministry of Finance, and the TIPS Clone instant-payments build is financed by an EUR 8m World Bank loan and delivered via Banca d'Italia — meaning EU-portal, TED and World Bank project/STEP feeds are mandatory sources for this cell, and national-portal-only monitoring would miss almost everything that matters.

Montenegro's donor-funded tender channel is a small, English-dominated, well-structured set of publication venues that sits almost entirely outside the national eProcurement system: TED and the EU Funding & Tenders Portal for IPA/PRAG contracts (with the EU Delegation and the Ministry of Finance CFCU as contracting authorities), ECEPP for EBRD client procurement, projects.worldbank.org plus Finances One for World Bank operations, UNDP's Montenegro RSS feed and UNGM for UN agencies, and WBIF/EIB for blended technical assistance. The single most on-target anchor right now is the World Bank's EUR 8m Financial Infrastructure Modernization and SEPA alignment (TIPS-clone) project, whose appraisal documentation names the payments-infrastructure work that will be tendered; its procurement plan is the highest-value next extraction. Local-language coverage is genuinely thin by nature of the channel — the only meaningful Montenegrin-language surface found is the Directorate for Public Procurement Policy's 'EU tenderi' category plus CFCU and Audit Authority material, which matter for award and execution intelligence rather than opportunity spotting. Commercial aggregators (dgMarket, TendersInfo and peers) duplicate these feeds behind paywalls and should be treated as non-collectable hints, never as sources.

Montenegro's commercial banks are private and, on the evidence of this run, publish essentially nothing about their procurement: NLB, Hipotekarna and Erste were fetched directly and none has a nabavka, tender, dobavljači or RFP section, and no ME bank was found issuing a 'poziv za dostavljanje ponuda' for technology — the phrase is used locally for share issues and real-estate disposals instead. The realistic source landscape for this cell is therefore a layered indirect one: the CBCG register of banks and UBCG (plus its 'Bankar' journal PDFs) as the actor-map pointers; EBRD's ECEPP and the EU Delegation's Montenegrin award notices as the only mechanisms that can force a private bank's sourcing into public view; Montenegroberza issuer filings and bank annual reports for contractual and outsourcing disclosures; and vendor-side press plus technical fingerprinting (an Asseco package id in the NLB Klik Crna Gora app listing is the clearest ME attribution found) as the highest-yield attribution route. The single biggest operational risk is that CKB — the market leader and most important buyer here — could not be read at all due to a TLS chain failure, which should be treated as a fixable client/config problem rather than a dead source.

For the foreign parents of Montenegro's banks there is no tender-notice layer to harvest: Erste, NLB, Addiko and OTP all buy centrally and none publishes an itemised competition feed covering the Montenegrin subsidiary. What exists instead is a three-tier landscape — onboarding gates (OTP's szállítóknak page routing into SAP Ariba; Erste Group Procurement in Vienna, which explicitly manages the entire external spend of all majority-owned group entities and publishes supplier terms, NDAs, audit questionnaires and scorecards), signal channels (group newsrooms at erstegroup.com, otpgroup.info and nlbgroup.com, plus sister-bank newsrooms such as otpbanka.hr that announce Montenegro-affecting decisions in Croatian), and disclosure mining (Addiko's Corporate Governance and Group Annual Reports, which confirm a Group procurement policy binding all entities above a threshold, and the EBA's DORA Register-of-Information regime, which inventories exactly these vendor relationships for the EU-supervised parents). The one genuine parent-level tender portal found is Turkish — Ziraat's ihale.ziraatbank.com.tr — and it needs a headless-browser retry before its category coverage can be judged. Local-language search was decisive but in an unexpected direction: Serbian queries produced only the actor map and the CBCG bank register, while every direct procurement source in this slice was reachable only in Hungarian, German, Slovenian or Turkish, and the bare English acronyms OTP and NLB are unusable, returning the Ontario Tenders Portal and the Northern Lighthouse Board respectively.

Supplier-side visibility in Montenegro is thin but structurally predictable: global OEMs (NCR Atleos, Diebold Nixdorf) almost never name Montenegrin buyers, while regional distributors and integrators do — Printec Montenegro (transaction automation since 2014), Asseco SEE via its Podgorica-area entity and the MoneyGet ATM network, Halcom in e-banking, and Payten/Monri in POS and e-commerce acquiring. Domestic integrators (Logate, ČIKOM, Amplitudo) publish contract-level detail, including values, in Montenegrin on their own sites, LinkedIn and eKapija, making local-language monitoring mandatory rather than optional. Where no announcement exists at all — which is the norm for core banking and digital onboarding — supplier attribution is still recoverable from unfalsifiable fingerprints such as mobile-app package IDs (e.g. NLB Podgorica's apps carry an Asseco package prefix) and hosting/subdomain evidence. Priority next steps are browser-grade retrieval of the vendor sites (printecgroup.com returned 403), a per-bank vendor attribution grid, and dedicated Montenegrin terminology for card personalisation and switch/processing, which remain unsearched.

Montenegro's payments-buyer landscape is small, register-transparent at the top and announcement-driven below it: the CBCG maintains authoritative registers of payment institutions and their agents (seven PIs observed, including Montenegro Transfers, PaySpot ME and Alta Pay Group), of payment systems, and of revoked authorisations, while the e-money register is presently empty — making it a market-entry tripwire rather than an inventory. Independent ATM deployment is a genuinely separate landscape here, with at least two non-bank fleet operators present (Euronet with a Montenegrin-language site, and Asseco/Payten's MoneyGet), and Pošta Crne Gore doubles as the largest non-bank payments distribution network and a contracting authority that publishes its own tenders. Formal demand signals concentrate in the CEJN e-procurement portal and in the World Bank-financed SEPA/TIPS-clone modernisation project, whose IFI procurement rules will expose supplier awards that domestic partnership deals never do. The weak flank is everything cash-side and processing-side: CIT operators, cash-centre contractors and the actual card processors behind each ME bank remain unidentified, and local-language queries need .me or 'Crna Gora' constraints because Serbian and Croatian results otherwise dominate.
